titre: The Trial That Made an Individual a Subject of International Law
accroche: On October 1, 1946, a tribunal convicts German leaders personally, not their State. Twenty-two years earlier, only a State could be tried.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 20, 1945, twenty-four dignitaries of the Nazi regime take their seats in the dock of a courtroom in Nuremberg. None of them appears in the name of Germany: each answers for his own acts. Until then, international law recognized only States as subjects: an individual could not be convicted under it, only his government.

## A Charter Signed in Six Weeks

On August 8, 1945, three months after the German surrender, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Provisional Government of the French Republic and the Soviet Union sign in London the charter that creates the International Military Tribunal. Its Article 6 lists three categories of crimes within its jurisdiction: crimes against peace (planning, preparing, initiating or waging a war of aggression or a war in violation of international treaties), war crimes, and crimes against humanity. The text names individuals, leaders, organizers or accomplices, never States.

The defense challenges this very principle: international law, it argues, binds only sovereign States; an official acting in the name of his State cannot answer for it personally, and a soldier carrying out an order merely applies the law of his country. The tribunal rejects the argument in its judgment of October 1, 1946: “Crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities, and only by punishing individuals who commit such crimes can the provisions of international law be enforced.” Twenty-two defendants are tried: one of the twenty-four indicted committed suicide before the trial opened, and another was found unfit to stand trial. Twelve are sentenced to death, three acquitted.

## A Principle That Outlives the Tribunal That Stated It

The International Military Tribunal tried only one case, and dissolved after its verdict. The principle it laid down did not stop with it: on December 11, 1946, the United Nations General Assembly unanimously adopts, in the presence of fifty-five member States, Resolution 95 (I), which affirms the principles of international law recognized by the charter and the judgment of Nuremberg. A little over a year after a Bavarian courtroom, the idea that an individual answers personally for an international crime becomes a principle recognized by the United Nations as a whole: before founding, decades later, the international criminal tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda, then the International Criminal Court.

carte.punch: A tribunal tried men, not a State, and it had never been done before.
carte.idee: On October 1, 1946, the Nuremberg tribunal convicts German leaders personally, rejecting the idea that only a State can answer for an international crime. Two months later, the UN adopts this principle unanimously.

quiz.question: Why does the Nuremberg tribunal reject the defense's argument that international law can only apply to States?
choix: Because the London Charter provides for a collective fine to be paid by the German State, which makes the argument moot
Because crimes under international law are committed by men, and only their individual punishment can enforce that law
Because Germany had lost its sovereignty through its surrender, and could therefore no longer invoke any legal argument
Because the defendants had already individually admitted guilt before the trial opened
quiz.explication: The tribunal states explicitly that crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities, and that only punishing individuals can enforce that law; neither a collective fine, nor the German surrender, nor a prior confession enters into its reasoning.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When is the charter creating the International Military Tribunal signed, and by whom?
choix: On October 1, 1946, in Nuremberg, by the four occupying powers
On August 8, 1945, in London, by the United States, the United Kingdom, France and the USSR
On November 20, 1945, in Geneva, by the League of Nations
On December 11, 1946, in New York, by the United Nations General Assembly
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The London Charter is signed on August 8, 1945 by the United States, the United Kingdom, the Provisional Government of the French Republic and the Soviet Union, three months after the German surrender.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many defendants are sentenced to death at the end of the Nuremberg trial, on October 1, 1946?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The judgment of October 1, 1946 sentences twelve of the twenty-two defendants tried to death, and acquits three; the other two indicted men were not tried.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which United Nations General Assembly resolution affirms the principles of the Nuremberg judgment, two months after the verdict?
choix: The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The General Assembly unanimously adopts, in the presence of fifty-five member States, Resolution 95 (I) of December 11, 1946, which affirms the principles recognized by the charter and the judgment of Nuremberg.
